newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 24.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

On the eve of talks with Queensland National Party Premier Rob Borbidge, Deputy Prime Minister and National Party Leader Tim Fischer has been isolated by the federal arm of his own party. While Fischer supports the 10-point plan put forward by Prime Minister John Howard, federal National Party president Don McDonald yesterday supported Borbidge's call for complete extinguishment of native title on pastoral leases. Page 1.

Liberal Party federal director Andrew Robb is expected to announce today that he will be taking a position in the private sector. Robb orchestrated the Coalition's landslide election win in 1996, using sophisticated U.S.-style campaign techniques and polling to counter the Labor Party's strengths. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard stepped in yesterday to retain funding for the Australian Film Commission and the Film Finance Commission following proposed budget cuts by the Treasury and the Department of Finance. The defence of the film budget is a major win for Communications and Arts Minister Richard Alston who has been under pressure to reduce assistance to the industry. Page 4.

The Metal Trades Industry Association has used a fortnight-long campaign at five Email plants in Victoria as a vehicle for a test case on "pattern" enterprise bargaining, which could disallow unions from taking protected industrial action in pursuit of common wage outcomes within an industry or multi-site company. The case will go before the Industrial Relations Commission in Melbourne today. Page 4.
THE AUSTRALIAN

The Australian Vice-Chancellors Committee has decided against supporting the use of student vouchers - a system that would direct funds to students rather than tertiary institutions - in its submission to the West review of higher education. The AVCC's submission also warns HECS contributions have reached the limits that students can afford. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard is expected to defend his 10-point plan in response to the High Court Wik decision today, telling Aboriginal leaders it cannot be watered down, and explaining to Queensland Premier Rob Borbidge that the plan will protect farmers and development on pastoral leases. Page 1.

The Victorian Supreme Court heard yesterday from Premier Jeff Kennett, as well as ACTU Secretary Bill Kelty and business leader Lindsay Fox, who gave character evidence to support disgraced former Coles Myer head Brian Quinn. Quinn was last week was convicted of conspiracy to fraud Coles of A$4.46 million. Page 1.

The Federation Centenary Convention held in Adelaide this week yesterday released a communique supporting an Australian head of state and identifying principles on which Australia should be based in the 21st century. The convention was attended by invited delegates ranging from former prime ministers to judges, scientists and students. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

New South Wales Attorney-General Jeff Shaw has made urgent inquiries to the Wood Royal Commission into the New South Wales Police Service after a Supreme Court judge ruled yesterday ten search warrants issued to commission investigators hoping to prosecute scores of corrupt police and pedophiles uncovered by the commission were so badly worded they were illegal. Page 1.

Australian lawyer Mark Plunkett, who conducted a war crimes tribunal in Cambodia, will act as a go-between in negotiations for peace on the Papua New Guinea island of Bougainville under federal government plans to push for peace and commit millions of dollars to boost reconstruction. Page 1.

CityRail's November timetable will be scrapped after it caused delays for thousands of commuters and cost State Rail chief executive Len Harper his job. The old timetable, to be reinstated from June, will dump up to 50 peak and off-peak services and offer longer trains to ensure there is no overcrowding. Page 3.

A New South Wales parliamentary committee consisting of editors, advertisers and representatives of the fashion industry will target anorexia, bulimia and the motivations that inspire young girls to want to be smaller. The committee will encourage the advertising industry and women's magazines to use larger women as models and has been given 12 months to find solutions. Page 3.
THE AGE

In a report tabled in the Victorian Parliament yesterday, State Auditor-General Ches Baragwanath said a judicial inquiry may be required to investigate the awarding of A$32 million of Metropolitan Ambulance Service contracts from 1993 to 1995. Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett has not ruled out the possibility of a royal commission into the allegations. Page 1.

Australian actor Mel Gibson, well-known in Hollywood for his clean-cut image, has angered the anti-tobacco lobby as his next role is that of a tobacco lobbyist who advocates the joys of cigarettes. The anti-smoking lobby has dismissed claims by the tobacco industry that the role signals rebellion against them - Gibson has reportedly quit a 40-a-day habit. Page 1.

New guidelines released yesterday by the National Health and Medical Research Council have urged doctors to become more aggressive in treating a deadly disease which is becoming more common among young children. Measures to combat meningococcal disease include buying powerful broad-spectrum antibiotics and emergency "black" bags to ensure prompt treatment. Page A3.

Heather Bell, spokeswoman for a support group for girls from St Catherine's children's home in Geelong who suffered widespread physical and emotional abuse in the 1950s and 60s, said group members will meet with Victorian Community Services Minister Deni Napthane on May 12 to seek support services for the former state wards, including counselling and help in tracing lost families. Page A3.
